questions.q: What are the four steps of the phase estimation circuit, in order?
options: Hadamards on the counting register, controlled-U^(2^k) applications, inverse QFT on the counting register, then measurement
Measurement, controlled-U, Hadamards, then QFT
Inverse QFT, Hadamards, measurement, then controlled-U
Controlled-U, measurement, Hadamards, then inverse QFT
questions.explain: The circuit superposes the counting qubits, kicks back phases via controlled-U^(2^k), decodes them with the inverse QFT, then measures to read off the estimate.

questions.q: In the phase-kickback derivation, after applying controlled-U with control (|0⟩+|1⟩)/√2 and target |ψ⟩ (where U|ψ⟩ = e^(iφ)|ψ⟩), what happens to the target register?
options: It comes out completely unchanged and disentangled, still exactly |ψ⟩ -- the phase lands on the control qubit instead
It becomes entangled with the control qubit and can no longer be factored out
It is destroyed and must be reinitialized before the next step
It picks up the phase e^(iφ) itself, while the control qubit is left unchanged
questions.explain: The algebra shows the joint state factors as [(|0⟩+e^(iφ)|1⟩)/√2] ⊗ |ψ⟩ -- the target register is unchanged, and the phase is 'kicked back' onto the control qubit.

questions.q: Why does counting qubit k control U^(2^k) specifically, rather than just U?
options: Because U^(2^k)|ψ⟩ = e^(2πiθ·2^k)|ψ⟩, so this doubling lets each successive counting qubit contribute one more bit of θ, building exactly the phase-encoded state the inverse QFT is designed to decode
Because applying U^(2^k) is always computationally cheaper than applying U once
It is an arbitrary convention with no mathematical necessity
Because U^(2^k) always equals the identity for k > 0
questions.explain: Repeated application of U multiplies the phase, so U^(2^k) contributes phase e^(2πiθ·2^k) -- exactly the structure needed to encode θ bit by bit across the counting register.

questions.q: Why is the inverse QFT the right operation to apply to the counting register in step 3?
options: After phase kickback, the counting register is in the exact superposition form (1/√(2^n))Σ e^(2πiθx)|x⟩ that the QFT encodes phases into -- so the inverse QFT decodes θ back out, directly reusing the Chapter 2 transform
The inverse QFT is applied only because it is computationally convenient, with no mathematical connection to the counting register's state
The inverse QFT is needed to initialize the counting qubits into superposition
The inverse QFT replaces the need for controlled-U gates entirely
questions.explain: Phase estimation's step 3 is literally the Chapter 2 Quantum Fourier Transform, applied in reverse, to decode the phase θ that was just encoded into the counting register's amplitudes.

questions.q: In the worked example with θ = 1/4 exactly and n = 2 counting qubits, what is the measurement outcome and why?
options: k = 1 is measured with probability exactly 1.0, because 1/4 lands exactly on the n=2 grid of representable values (k/4), leaving no probability to leak into other outcomes
All four outcomes k=0,1,2,3 are equally likely, each with probability 0.25
k = 3 is measured with probability 1.0, since 3/4 is the closest representable value
The outcome is undefined because θ = 1/4 cannot be represented with 2 bits
questions.explain: Because 1/4 = 0.01 in binary is exactly representable with 2 bits, the computed probabilities are P(k=1)=1.000000 and all others 0 -- a fully deterministic result.
